subject: chemistry

items.q: A burning splint is held at the open end of a test tube of an unknown gas. Which observation shows that the gas is hydrogen?
items.correct: The gas burns rapidly with a pop.
items.misconception: The splint goes out straight away.
items.why: Students learn that oxygen is needed for burning and conclude that any gas which is not oxygen must extinguish a flame, forgetting that hydrogen is itself a fuel that burns. Hydrogen is flammable. When the burning splint meets it at the mouth of the tube the hydrogen itself burns rapidly, and the sound of that rapid burning is the pop.
items.random_wrong: The splint glows brighter and relights.

items.q: A student has collected a test tube of gas and wants to test whether it is hydrogen. What should the student do?
items.correct: Hold a burning splint at the open end of the test tube.
items.misconception: Insert a glowing splint into the tube of the gas.
items.why: Both splint tests use a wooden splint, and both give a flame at the end, so students remember 'splint' but not which state it is in or which gas gives which result. Two different splint states give two different tests: a burning splint at the mouth of the tube tests for hydrogen (it burns with a pop), while a glowing splint inserted into the tube tests for oxygen (it relights).
items.random_wrong: Lower a lit splint into the tube and see if it goes out.

items.q: A student holds a burning splint at the open end of a test tube that should contain hydrogen, but hears no pop. Which is the most likely explanation?
items.correct: The gas escaped from the tube before the splint was used.
items.misconception: Hydrogen does not burn, so no sound is ever produced.
items.why: Students learn that oxygen is needed for burning and conclude that any gas which is not oxygen must extinguish a flame, forgetting that hydrogen is itself a fuel that burns. Hydrogen is flammable. When the burning splint meets it at the mouth of the tube the hydrogen itself burns rapidly, and the sound of that rapid burning is the pop.
items.random_wrong: The splint should have been glowing rather than burning.

items.q: Which observation shows that a test tube contains oxygen?
items.correct: A glowing splint relights in the gas.
items.misconception: A burning splint gives a pop in the gas.
items.why: The pop is the most memorable observation in the whole topic, so it gets attached to the gas students hear about most often, which is oxygen. The pop belongs to hydrogen only. Oxygen is identified by a glowing splint relighting when it is inserted into a test tube of the gas.
items.random_wrong: The gas burns with a bright flame itself.

items.q: A glowing splint is inserted into a test tube of oxygen and relights. Which statement about this result is correct?
items.correct: The oxygen lets the splint burn again; the splint is the fuel.
items.misconception: The oxygen itself burns, which is why a flame appears.
items.why: A flame appears the moment the splint enters the oxygen, so the gas looks like the thing that has caught fire. Oxygen is not a fuel. The splint is the fuel; the oxygen lets the glowing splint burn again, which is why it relights.
items.random_wrong: The gas is hydrogen, since hydrogen relights a splint.

items.q: Tube 1 gives a pop when a burning splint is held at its open end. Tube 2 relights a glowing splint. Which gases are in the tubes?
items.why: The pop is the most memorable observation in the whole topic, so it gets attached to the gas students hear about most often, which is oxygen. The pop belongs to hydrogen only. Oxygen is identified by a glowing splint relighting when it is inserted into a test tube of the gas.

items.q: Which reagent is used in the test for carbon dioxide?
items.correct: An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide
items.misconception: An aqueous solution of sodium hydroxide
items.why: Students know limewater is alkaline and generalise from 'an alkali' to 'any alkali', losing the specific reagent. The named reagent is an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide (limewater). Sodium hydroxide solution is not the reagent for this test.
items.random_wrong: A solution of solid calcium carbonate

items.q: Carbon dioxide is bubbled through limewater. What is observed?
items.misconception: The limewater turns colourless and clear.
items.why: Students use 'clear' loosely to mean 'changed', and limewater starts out colourless, so the word is used for the wrong end of the change. Limewater is clear and colourless before the test. A positive result is the opposite: it becomes milky and cloudy so you can no longer see through it.
items.random_wrong: The limewater turns from blue to red.

items.q: A student shakes a gas sample with limewater in a stoppered tube and the limewater turns milky. Their partner says the test does not count because the gas was not bubbled through. Who is right?
items.correct: The student, because the gas can be shaken with or bubbled through.
items.misconception: The partner: only bubbling through limewater is a valid test.
items.why: Bubbling through a delivery tube is the version usually demonstrated, so it becomes the only remembered method. The specification allows both: when carbon dioxide is shaken with or bubbled through limewater, the limewater turns milky (cloudy).
items.random_wrong: The partner, because a positive result should leave the limewater clear.

items.q: Damp litmus paper is put into a test tube of chlorine gas. What is observed?
items.correct: The paper is bleached and turns white.
items.misconception: The paper turns red and then stays red.
items.why: Litmus paper is met first as an acid-base indicator, so any colour change on litmus is read as an acid-base result rather than as bleaching. The result recorded for chlorine is bleaching: the colour is removed from the paper and the paper turns white.
items.random_wrong: The paper changes only if it is dry.

items.q: A student tests a tube of chlorine using dry litmus paper and sees no change. What should the student do next?
items.correct: Repeat the test using damp litmus paper.
items.misconception: Record that the gas cannot be chlorine.
items.why: In other indicator work the paper is used dry, and 'damp' looks like an incidental practical detail rather than part of the method. The specification states that damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas. If the paper is dry the expected bleaching may not be seen, so the paper must be damp.
items.random_wrong: Repeat the test using dry blue litmus paper.

items.q: A colourless gas is tested. A burning splint at the open end of the tube goes out with no pop, a glowing splint does not relight, and damp litmus paper put into the gas turns white. Which conclusion is best supported?
items.correct: The gas is chlorine, since damp litmus paper is bleached white.
items.misconception: No conclusion is possible until the test is repeated with dry paper.
items.why: In other indicator work the paper is used dry, and 'damp' looks like an incidental practical detail rather than part of the method. The specification states that damp litmus paper is put into the chlorine gas. If the paper is dry the expected bleaching may not be seen, so the paper must be damp.
items.random_wrong: The gas is oxygen, because a splint gives no pop in oxygen.

items.correct: An aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide.
items.misconception: Limewater is a solution of calcium carbonate.
items.why: The name 'lime' is used loosely for several calcium compounds, and students associate the milky test result with carbonate, so they attach the carbonate name to the reagent as well. The reagent used in the test is an aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide. That is what the specification names as limewater.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is a burning splint being extinguished a test for carbon dioxide?
items.correct: No: the test for carbon dioxide uses limewater, which turns milky (cloudy).
items.misconception: If a burning splint goes out in a gas, that shows the gas is carbon dioxide.
items.why: Carbon dioxide is met in the context of fire extinguishers, so 'puts the flame out' feels like its identifying property. Many gases fail to support combustion, so a splint going out identifies nothing. Carbon dioxide is identified by shaking it with or bubbling it through limewater and seeing the limewater turn milky.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does limewater change colour like an indicator in the carbon dioxide test?
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide is acidic, so the limewater changes colour, turning red.
items.why: Solutions that change on adding a gas are usually indicators in students' experience, so a colour-change answer is offered instead of a cloudiness answer. Limewater is not being used as an indicator here. The recorded observation is that the limewater turns milky (cloudy).
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.8.2 Identification of common gases
